And now whether they would be fired in single launches or in salvos, that will depend on the target chosen and on the situation at the front line. It is a fire support weapon, as I said, which would be fired across one's troops and therefore calls for a certain degree of certainty, since one would be firing across one's own troops. There has to be a degree of safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what are rocket engines initiated with?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are initiated instantaneously with a small device called Shafiro's [phoen] head or something similar. It's a small device which on the basis of -- which ignites it with electrical resistance. It's all done electrically, basically. It's a device which has a number of options depending on the target that you've chosen, but at any rate, it's being ignited electrically.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused repeat, please, what he referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that the piezoelectrical effect?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: We're not familiar with the term.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Piezo. Piezo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, very well. Does that ensure the simultaneity, and can the simultaneous launch be done without any delays if this sort of electrical igniter is used?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is the effect of electrical ignition on the simultaneity of launch? Does the electrical impulse reach it simultaneously at a distance of 10 centimetres?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, this is again leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You could have stopped at the first sentence. The last part was leading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think Ms. Subotic, given her expertise, can be led in anyway. I'm simply asking, since the simultaneity of launch was challenged during the cross-examination, I'm simply asking what sort of effect would this piezoelectrical ignition have on the launch being simultaneous? Does it ensure that it is simultaneous or does it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, the only evidence there has been of this piezoelectrical effect is from the accused himself, so any question that has this in it is already -- has this built-in assumption that the witness has testified about this and it's leading. She has not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't remember having heard about piezo so far either. So the question is: What is the effect of electrical ignition on the simultaneity of launch? Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That's a good formulation of my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course I can. What arises from your question, to my understanding, is the following: The ignition itself, the electrical ignition, when it is being tested, we're talking about milliseconds of difference which is a margin that is allowed, in technical terms, by that PKP document. If the electricity does not ignite the device within these bounds that were tested, then it will not ignite it at all. The question is quite simple. You either have the electricity or you don't, and the order of magnitude of dispersion and of reaction to that impulse is measured in milliseconds. Please don't ask me to pick out the information from the PKP off the cuff because I don't know it by heart, but the PKP is there, and you can consult it for any of the products, for any of the assets. I'm sure that your department for co-operation will deliver it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was also challenged was that the police alerted the population not to join the queues for water.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's footnote 102, page 82, paragraph 56. That's where I'd like to direct the attention of the Trial Chamber to. I said that's footnote 102. Can we see that in e-court, paragraph 56.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Footnote 202, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 82. In English it's 37.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think this is in the document D3542.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mortar report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you. Footnotes, please. 202.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I'd just like to put on the record that the accused stated that what was also challenged was that the police alerted population not to join the queue for water. That's not correct. What was challenged was that the fact that the police alerted the population not to join the queue or warned the population was due to the fact that they had been tipped off in advance. That was the assertion that was challenged.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the difference lies in the fact that what is described by her here are soldiers, but the fact of the matter is, do we have evidence to the effect that this was something that occurred routinely? That's not something that we could conclude on the basis of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this statement in footnote 202 something that you bore in mind?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that's why it was cited here and quoted. The statement reads: "That morning as we headed towards Oslobodilaca Sarajeva Street, we were stopped by three --" is this what we're talking about; right? "... three Bosnian soldiers who told us Dobrinja was a dangerous place because of intense shelling and constant gunfire. They tried to persuade us --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Not to go there."

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was waiting for the transcript. "... to persuade us not to go there. But since we did not want to give up, they told us that if we heard gunfire, we had to head home immediately. They also told us that if we heard a shell fall, other shells usually followed."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I will not trouble you any longer. Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Judge Morrison has a few questions for you, Mrs. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mrs. Subotic, your theory is that persons who were already dead were brought to the scene of the explosions to be placed amongst the people killed by the explosions in order to amplify the scale of the killing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, do you mean the Markale I incident of the 5th of February? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, video footage points in that direction. The number of deaths which we looked at a couple of days ago, it was given in that table, was a terrible consequence that we cannot at all view within the limits of the firepower of this weapon. That's one fact. We tested, as you were probably able to see, the estimate of the number of deaths. Not taking into consideration only the limits of the firepower of the weapon, we looked into other elements, there are two or three ways in which it was possible to check the number of deaths, and it was all very different from what was given in the table as the official number of dead, the official number of fatalities which you could see ranged between 150 and 300-odd. We observed that there were indications, and we documented them, and in this way we pointed to our inability to in any way bring together, on the one hand, the number of fatalities with, on the other, the firepower of the weapon and the physical evidence on the site. And everything that we observed, we noted down in our report. There were also forensic examinations that were consistent with our position, and we cited them all. We simply could not overlook something that we observed in the course of our investigation and review of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: So is the answer to my question "yes"?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: It would therefore be necessary for people who are already dead and who had suffered wounds consistent with a mortar explosion to be stored somewhere in readiness to be brought to the scene. That must follow from the theory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But I have to say that the injuries caused by mortar shells were an everyday occurrence, because that was simply the weapon that was most frequently used in the clashes in that region, as we know full well. At the very start of the footage, I drew the attention to the military lorry which was there even before the evacuation. We can see it on Marsala Tita Street at the very start of the evacuation. There were elements in the footage that I viewed which were indicative of a great many things, but I do not want to construct a story on the basis of something that does not allow us to be conclusive in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But nevertheless, your theory is that this was a deliberate act resulting from a conspiracy on behalf of somebody to add to the numbers killed in the explosion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It fits with the entire context provided by the physical evidence above all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Then in respect to the -- if that theory is right, the bodies, the people who were already dead before the explosion, their deaths could not have been previously reported or any medical examination conducted upon those bodies, because otherwise the conspiracy would be immediately foiled, because a relative who, for instance, knew that his brother, father, mother, or sister had been killed in a mortar explosion several days beforehand would be surprised to read in the press that they had been killed at Markale I and would be likely to raise a query, would they not?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume that they would. However, in the Markale II incident, we have one fatality who was listed as having been killed in that incident, whereas we found a document which stated that he had been killed in fighting and that he was a BH Army soldier. I'm citing this example, because it was a document that happened to be in our hands. I suppose that the case would indeed be as you put it. There was another instance, which I think we cited in our report, of a fatality. The body was in the morgue and had been -- or, rather, that had been on the counter of one of the stalls, and by looking at her you would say that she was dead already at the market-place. However, what I want to say is that the lists that were drawn up revealed a -- what was an utter confusion. We found it very difficult to follow the lists drawn up in hospitals, the lists of those killed. It is really incredible the condition the lists were in. There were pages missing, and we were at great pains to sort through the papers that were official, let alone others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: But you have agreed, I think, with me previously that you have never experienced a visit to a scene of a mortar explosion where people were killed or injured in person, and that you have no forensic medical training. Are both of those observations correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they are, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: And lastly, there was a query about whether or not dead or injured people should be moved first. I simply raise this: Would you accept or not that if you inexpertly move an injured person, you might do them more harm than good, for instance, if that person had suffered neck or spinal injuries?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's what we're all taught at first aid courses. Yes, you're right. Inexpertly helping people can be very dangerous, and we shouldn't do anything unless we're sure what the nature of the injury is. Everybody with a driving licence had to go through such a course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your evidence, Mrs. Subotic. Thank you for your coming to The Hague yet again to give it. Now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me the opportunity to present my work.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If your Excellency thinks of break, I think you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the Chamber is minded to take a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. President. Just for the record, Mrs. Subotic as she was exiting the courtroom attempted to give me a piece of paper on which were some calculations and I declined her offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for an hour and resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Katanic, please be seated and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it you understand my words in the language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Katanic.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to perhaps move a bit closer to the microphone, but do sit comfortably, and both you and I should speak at a moderate pace and make a sufficiently long break between question and answer to enable the interpreters to interpret everything.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: A few days ago when I went to see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And before that did you give a statement to our team which we reviewed before we met now?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was in December.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D07007, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see that statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed it?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I read and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just wait a moment before you start speaking after me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown page 2 so as to enable him to identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully reflect what you said to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions now, would your answers be essentially the same?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, they would.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I tender this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D3561, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read the summary of Mr. Katanic's statement in English. [In English] In July 1995, Dane Katanic was President of the Executive Board of Skelani municipality. Mr. Katanic met with President Karadzic in late June and on 11th of July, 1995, to express his concern over the attacks by Bosnian Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave into Skelani and the vulnerability of Skelani to Muslim attacks. On the evening of 11th of July, 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica, Mr. Katanic attended a meeting in Bratunac at the invitation of Miroslav Deronjic. Deronjic informed him that President Karadzic had appointed him civilian commissioner for Srebrenica. There were disagreements between those from Skelani and Deronjic over the personnel who should be in charge of Srebrenica municipality and how to organise things there. Deronjic agreed to make an appointment for a meeting at President Karadzic's office to discuss these matters. On July the 14th, 1995, Mr. Katanic attended a meeting in Pale with Miroslav Deronjic and President Karadzic. Momcilo Krajisnik also participated in part of the meeting. Mr. Katanic objected to Deronjic being appointed civilian commissioner when he was from another municipality, Bratunac. They discussed this matter for two or three hours. President Karadzic insisted that Deronjic should be the head of the War Presidency and that there should be nine members. Deronjic provided the names to President Karadzic, who accepted them. During this meeting there was no discussion about any killings of prisoners from Srebrenica. President Karadzic came to Srebrenica a few days before the fall of Knin in late July or early August 1995. They again discussed whether Skelani and Srebrenica would be one or two municipalities and the implication -- and the implication of that. There was no discussion about any killings of prisoners from Srebrenica. [Interpretation] This was a brief summary. At this moment I have no questions for Mr. Katanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, would you kindly ask the witness to read paragraph 5 of his statement and expand a little bit -- expand a little bit about that, what he meant there, because I don't follow well. Mr. Katanic, do you see paragraph 5? We can collapse the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I read it out? "In the morning of the 11th of July, 1995, after victims on the Serb side on the 9th and 10th of July, I went to Pale with Milenko Canic and Momcilo Cvjetinovic to tell President Karadzic that if the line between Srebrenica and Skelani were to be pierced, nothing would be left to defend Skelani. President Karadzic listened to us but he gave no indication of his plans. He said that our positions around Srebrenica were being shelled." I could only add here: "By the international community." Am I to explain anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Our position, Srebrenica, was being shelled by international community or NATO," that's what you meant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what did you mean that in the morning of 11th July there had been some Serbian victims? Or Serbian victims on the 9th and 10th. What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say that there was fighting, and on the 9th and 10th some Serbs got killed, and I was afraid that the lines would yield. From the site of the fighting to Skelani there were -- the distance was about 30 kilometres. There was nobody left there. Everybody had gone. So if the -- if our defence line were to be pierced, then Skelani would have been taken. That's why we went to Pale to inform the president of our opinion and our fear made us go to Pale to inform the president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you know or did you not at the time that an operation by the Drina Corps was taking place at the place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew, but I didn't know that it was not an option for the lines to yield. I didn't know that nothing bad would happen to the Serbian people, and I don't believe anybody of us there knew that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You met Mr. Karadzic twice on that day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We met on the 11th at Pale.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I understood. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No more questions, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. As you noted, your evidence in chief in this case, Mr. Katanic, has been admitted in writing, that is, through your statement. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon, everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, just to follow up on what you just been asked by the President, when you're talking about Serb victims, we are talking about Serbs that died in the -- in the occasion of military operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you. On 17 September 2009, you gave an interview. You were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor. You told the truth during that interview; right?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I've always told the truth, and I'm telling the truth now, the truth about what I remembered and what I was able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: All right. So in interview you said that you joined the SDS in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, I think I joined the SDS in 1992. It may have been a month earlier or a month later, but I don't think that's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: In April 1992, the Serb municipality of Skelani was established, and you were appointed as the first President of the Executive Board of the municipality Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Correct. I went to Skelani in April, and started working in mid-April 1992 as President of the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 17477, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you probably recognise this document. This is 16 of June, 1992, appointment of the War Commission in the municipality of Skelani. Do you recognise your signature at the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Of course I recognise it. It bears my signature too.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you were also member of the War Commission starting from 16 of June, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: This is not a war commission but of a totally different body which is called "ratno predsjednistvo" in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "Ratno povjerenistvo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which means?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, yeah, that's exactly -- what does it mean in English? I'm not sure. The translation we have indicates "War Commission."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Both words "komisija" and "povjerenistvo" are translated as "commission" into English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, it is difficult to translate differently, but the word "povjerenistvo" stems from the word "povjerenje," "trust, confidence." [In English] "Entrusted by the central organ," something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This body was established and Dragan Djokanovic was the wartime commissioner for the Birac region for five or six municipalities, and based on the then laws and regulations, an assessment of the needs was made and it was decided to establish this wartime commission. Dragan Djokanovic was in charge of the Birac region, and he was a member of every wartime commission of the municipality, and apart from him there were some four or five more members per municipality. I was one of the members as stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in your interview, at page 13 you said this, and I quote: "Ever since 1998 or 1999, I was forbidden by international law any work in municipality and government bodies." Now, I'm asking you, you were referring here to a decision of the Office of the High Representative of the BiH to ban you from political activities?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I mean the officials of the international community. At that time, there was an appellate subcommission or something. I'm not sure what role they had. I'm not familiar with their organisation, but the representative of the international community banned me from -- from political activities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last sentence with the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the last sentence, because the translator couldn't catch up.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I was saying that the ban was lifted in 2006, and it was imposed in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I -- can I ask - I'm sorry, I keep making this mistake - the admission of the document we discussed a minute ago, 65 ter 17477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6331, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, moving on, on July 1995, in your statement at paragraph 6 you said that in the evening of the 11th of July, after the fall of Srebrenica, you were called to a meeting in Bratunac. Now, at the meeting, Deronjic informed you that he had been appointed civilian commissioner for Srebrenica. In your -- in your interview, in more details than in your statement, you discussed the disputes and disagreements between the Skelani delegation on the one hand, meaning you, Milenko Canic, and Momcilo Cvjetinovic, and Deronjic on the other side, and you expressed your disagreement because you thought that it was up to the political leadership in Skelani to be in charge of Srebrenica, and not Deronjic, who was from Bratunac; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, in your interview, you also said the following at page 33: "We find out that Miroslav of course had more influence. He was closer to Radovan. We could express our -- that we were unhappy but couldn't do much more about it." So if I understand correctly, you could express your disappointment, but there was not much you could do because Deronjic was closer to Mr. Karadzic. It is correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, who was closer than the other, I thought that Radovan respected Miroslav because he was the deputy president of the party for the Birac region. So naturally he would have been closer to the president than the rest of us who were mere members in a region such as Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, two days later, you kept discussing this matter, and you drove together with Momcilo Cvjetinovic and Milenko Canic. You drove to Pale to meet Karadzic and Deronjic, as you said at paragraph 7. Now, in that context, you were informed that Deronjic would have been the head of the Srebrenica War Presidency; right?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And again, you tried to show your disappointment for that decision. There was a discussion, and then at the end Deronjic gave to Mr. Karadzic a list of names that, and I read what you said in your interview: "None of us had any influence in terms of one single name for the War Presidency." Correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Correct. The president asked Mr. Deronjic to make a list of nine names, which he did. After a long discussion, after many comments, suggestions, remarks, Miroslav made a list of names the president accepted, and they were the members of the wartime Presidency of Skelani municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And that was the 14 of July; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: In any event, you and Cvjetinovic made it to the War Presidency and you were part of it. You were appointed as member of it. But again in your interview, you explained that Deronjic was the one with the real power, the one linked to Karadzic, and you said at page 41: "You know, Miroslav Deronjic was a link between him," meaning Mr. Karadzic, "and all the others of us. As long as the War Presidency existed, he was the one to make decision." So it was Deronjic and not you who was the one to take the decision because he was close and linked to Mr. Karadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic took decisions. Of course we played our part. But not because he was close to Karadzic, because at the time it was his position. In professional terms, he was president of the SDS for the region, and clearly Deronjic had more of a say than I did, because I was a mere member. I was rank and file, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Costi, I'm not sure we heard the answer from the first part of your question. Mr. Katanic, is it true that you and Mr. Cvjetinovic were appointed as members of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. The decision clearly shows that we were members, and the decision was public and available to -- accessible to everybody, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, although you didn't mention it in your statement, in your interview you explained that on 13 of July you went to Bratunac with Momcilo Cvjetinovic and Milenko Canic. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: That's correct. We were in Bratunac indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you went there in the morning, and you came back late in the afternoon; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: We went there in the morning in order to get there in time. We wanted to see the president in Pale and talk to him about the appointments and the functioning of the municipality. Miroslav was appointed as the civilian commissioner. We had a meeting. We left in the morning. Pale's not far. We arrived in Bratunac in the afternoon, and then we came back. I don't know exactly when we arrived, when we returned. In any case, we made it there and back on the same day. So from Skelani to Bratunac and back all on the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And just to make it clear, so on the 13th you went to Bratunac in the morning, if I understand your testimony which reflects what you said in interview, you went there because you said you thought that you would have had the meeting with Karadzic that day, and that for some reason the meeting didn't take place so you drove back to Skelani; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you spent some times at the SDS office that day; right?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: We had to go to the SDS office. Where else would we have found Miroslav? We were there in the office. I don't know for how long, but, yes, we were there. We were there long enough to learn that we wouldn't go to Pale, that a new meeting would be scheduled when conditions allowed for that meeting to be scheduled with President in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, in your interview you also described -- you were asked about the event in Bratunac on 13 July, and you talked about organised activities for the transportation of Muslims from Srebrenica, Potocari, and Bratunac, and you said at page 43: "There were organised activities and transportation of people. Buses were coming from Zvornik, Bratunac. Petrol was needed and diesel." Is it correct? Do you stand by what you said?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by that because that's how it was. People were transported by buses, and there's nothing there that is not well known, that was covered up.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you -- you saw those buses, and you're referring to buses passing by Bratunac, or you also saw buses stopping in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Sir, I did not watch. There was no need for me to observe the buses. I didn't spot them either stopping or passing through. I was in Bratunac. I could see that there was a lot of people. There were buses which passed by, but I didn't notice whether they stopped or double parked or stopped for a short while and then continued. It was not up to me to watch. There was no need for me to watch. I don't know what to say. I was not that interested. I had arrived to go to Pale. I wasn't there to count buses and to see whether they were stopping or passing through or double parking. There was somebody in charge for -- of that, and they did their job. I am not such a busybody to be looking where I'm not supposed to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I understand you weren't there to look at buses, and I understand it probably wasn't even your task to look at buses, but I don't understand what you said when you said that you were not looking where you were not supposed to look.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, now you are saying that I was there to watch whether a bus stopped or didn't stop or double parked and then proceeded. You're asking me questions that doesn't make too much sense. They don't mean much. I don't know what your questions mean. What do you mean when you ask me whether I saw if the buses had stopped or not? I don't know what those questions mean to you. They don't mean anything to me, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: May I -- may I help about -- witness is getting -- or probably Mr. Costi is getting different translations, because witness didn't say that he was not supposed to watch, but he said that he was not there to -- for that purpose. Didn't intend to count and to --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, if I look at page 66, the last line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he's referring to that. There was some slight translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: That's possible, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: In any event, I'm not suggesting you were there to count buses and I'm not asking you were to report exactly where and which bus and whatever. I'm saying that if we look at what was happening on that day, and we heard testimonies in this Chamber, in this courtroom, that there were thousand of Muslim prisoners at that time in Bratunac, I wonder whether you notice anything, and how can you say that it wasn't something that mattered to you?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know whether there were thousands of them. I personally don't think that there were thousands of prisoners in Bratunac. Believe me, I don't know. I cannot go that way. I did not see that. It was wartime. There are always people in the street. I didn't go there to observe people in the street, to take stock of the situation. I am familiar with Bratunac, and things were happening the way they were. I was on my way to Pale. I dropped by the SDS office. I learned that we would not be proceeding towards Pale, and as far as I was concerned, my business in Bratunac was finished. I don't know how much time we spent there, if we met somebody or not. Maybe we had a cup of coffee or -- I don't know. There were no bars or pubs there. There was no place where you could go and have a bite to eat or a glass to drink. I did pass through Bratunac, and if there were buses there, of course I saw them, but it was not my purpose. This was not my intention. I didn't go to Bratunac to observe buses at all. I don't know if you understand what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you know Milenko Katanic, because I believe he's a relative of yours; right?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I know him. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So in his testimony in this case, which is P04374 at paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Did we hear his answer, whether he's related to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am related to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, he testified and he said at paragraph 79 of his statement that there were buses with prisoners in various streets of the town. The prisoners were held in the school and the stadium, and the citizens from Bratunac were concerned for their security in light of the amount of prisoners detained there. Now, again I understand you weren't there to look at buses, but it strikes me as surprising that you spent time at the SDS office and you haven't had the opportunity to discuss the issue or to be concerned with the issue yourself.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Why would I discuss those issues with anybody? Please tell me. Pray tell me, why would I ever talk to anybody about that? At that time I did not discuss the whereabouts of those people and who they were. Pray tell me, why would I discuss that matter with anybody?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Because it was a reason for major concern in the whole town at that point, and it's surprising that you went and went back to Skelani without noticing the details of what happened.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, people were concerned there from 1990. They're still concerned. In 1992, people were dying. It is not that only in 1995 something happened. People led a good life. They went to work. They came back. They went to football matches. They went to the theatre. And then in 1995 all of a sudden something happened. From 1992 we buried our people. We bled, we died on both sides. We were at war in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995. Of course we were concerned all that time. We were also concerned in 1995. Of course we were, but we were also concerned in 1992 and every day in 1993, 1994, 1995. We were always concerned. We are still concerned to this very day. And if you want to put it in a context of a good life and at one point we all became concerned, that's -- that's a nonsense. We were all concerned all the time. Of course we were concerned. But that concern of ours has never stopped, and that's the whole essence. You're asking me, trying to portray our life as being good and then I arrived in Bratunac and something was going on. This is a normal situation, and it has been that way since 1992, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I suggest something? Mr. Costi is assuming that both the prisoners and Mr. Katanic were in Bratunac at the same time. Why wouldn't he give us a time-frame and tell us when the prisoners arrived and to -- up to which point was Mr. Katanic in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I don't think it was appropriate at this time. We can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, it's interesting you mention 1992, because in 1992, in exactly the same locations in Bratunac, in a slightly similar situation, if you wish, prisoners --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Is the witness from Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: No, he's not, Your Honour, from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very similar incident took place in Bratunac with prisoners detained at the stadium, at the school. They were beaten. They were killed. And as you said, you were concerned, so probably you knew about it even if you were not from Bratunac, and you probably were not there in 1992. Then all of a sudden in 1995 you go to Bratunac. You spend there, as I understood you said, you got there in the morning and you came back the same -- later the same day in the afternoon. All this is going on. You recognise and you see that there is an organised transportation, but when I ask you whether you notice and what you saw, you say, "I wasn't there for that. That wasn't my business."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: So, Mr. Costi, what is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. No, the question is whether he actually saw something. And I'm insisting on this because I believe this is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what do you suppose I may have seen? I really don't know. What was I supposed to see? And you know I saw it, and I don't want to tell you. Pray tell me. Pray enlighten me.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me move on to another topic. Now, on 13 July, the same day, you heard of the killings at the Kravica warehouse. In the interview that you gave to the Prosecution, you explained that you were informed because one of your men, or one man from Skelani, Krsto, was killed. And this is page 45 of your interview. Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you also heard that over a thousand prisoners were executed that day; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I did not hear that. I don't know that they were executed. Perhaps you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So you're saying that today here you do not know whether prisoners were executed at the Kravica warehouse? Is this your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: The question as you have phrased it now is completely different. If you want me to tell what I know, I will tell you, but don't phrase your questions differently. In the first question you asked me whether I know that over a thousand people were executed, and now you want me to say that I don't know that people were executed. Your questions are phrased differently. They're two different questions. And if that is the gist of your exercise, but if you want me to tell the truth, if you are keen on learning the truth, I am here to help you, because I -- I have sworn to tell the truth and now you're forcing me not to tell the truth or not to give you any information for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no. Rest assured, Mr. Katanic, there's nothing that you should be concerned about. To the first question you answered that you didn't know that there was execution at the time, and the second question was now do you know that there was execution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I apologise. No. I apologise. The Prosecutor, as far as I understood, asked me if I knew whether over 1.000 were shot dead on that day. I don't know that on that day over 1.000 were shot dead. And then in the second question he asked me, "Are you saying that you do not know that people were executed there." So these are two different questions and they have nothing to do what -- with each other. Of course I know that people were killed there, but I don't know that over a thousand were shot dead on that particular day, and on that particular day I didn't know that. That's the gist of my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well. I'm sorry if there was some confusion, but I understood your testimony saying that you don't know now that people were executed there. That's why I asked you whether you know now. And I understand from the rest of your testimony now that you, yes, can see that you today know that people were executed there. Now, what --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript. Transcript. Line 8. What is missing is: "I did not know on that day that people were killed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I didn't know the number. Certainly I was not aware of the number that the Prosecutor has now mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: So did you know or you didn't on the evening of the 13th that people were executed and killed -- or killed at the Kravica warehouse? Let me put it properly. Executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, I'm still confused as to whether the witness has testified that knew or he didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: On the 11th -- on the 13th of July, at that time, that people were executed at Kravica warehouse. No matter the numbers. I'm just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not know that on the 13th people were executed in Kravica. What I knew is the following: I heard that a Serbian soldier Krsto had been killed. I heard that because he hailed from Skelani and I was told that. I was told that the Muslims who were there snatched Krsto's rifle and killed him with it, and then another soldier came, grabbed that rifle from him and unrest followed. And that's all that I knew on at that day that had to do with Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Can I ask you what kind of unrest followed as far as you knew at that time?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: That there was shooting and killing, but when, how, and how many, that I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, as to the when, you probably should because you were informed on the 13th that one man from Skelani was murdered that day. Therefore, the when must be on the 13. As to the how, what was -- what was told? What was told to you? What did you know? How many people were killed in this unrest?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: To this very day I don't know how many people got killed during the unrest, and on the 13th, how was I supposed to know? Please enlighten me. If you say that I was supposed to know, then please enlighten me. How was I supposed to know that? Go ahead, be my guest.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Do you know Milenko Trifunovic?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And you know, don't you, that in September 2009, the BiH state court convicted him of genocide for taking part to the execution in the Kravica warehouse as a commander of the 3rd Skelani Platoon, which was part of the Skelani Battalion from your own little town. So what I'm asking you is whether you were only informed that one man that happened -- from Skelani that happened to be there was killed or whether you were actually told that independent -- the Skelani Independent Battalion was actually there shooting prisoners together with Milenko Trifunovic at that time.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, when you asked me about Milenko, you put it to me that I know that he was convicted by a court. I don't know that. I know that he's serving a sentence. Second of all, I only heard that on the 13th, Krsto was killed in Bratunac. I don't know how. And that is all I know. I didn't know that Milenko was there, Milenko Trifunovic. I didn't know that he opened fire on them or not. Please do not put it to me that I knew things if I didn't know things. I didn't know then. I don't know to this very day that the court in Bosnia found him guilty of something. It is not my job to follow those developments. It's your job. You're supposed to know who was convicted of -- of what and when and where. I have another job. I make my living in a different way. Please do not put words into my mouth. Please do not tell me that I know or knew something that I don't know and didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, when you do not know, it is sufficient for you to say you don't know. Rest assured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a confusion in the transcript. Mr. Katanic said, "I know he was found guilty in -- at the court in Bosnia, but I don't know why," and this is the essence of his answer. This is the crux. And -- what I'm reading here is that he did know, didn't know. Why --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor says that I know, and I don't know, and don't put words into my mouth. Don't tell me that I know things that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm asking if you know. I'm not putting any word in what you're saying. I'm asking you whether you know that he was convicted of genocide, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, and I'm not assuming you know. I'm asking you whether you know. So these are questions, not statements. Nobody's trying to tell anything. So why were you surprised when you were told that one man from Skelani was actually murdered there if you didn't know, as I understand you just said, that the Skelani Platoon was there?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the Skelani Battalion was a unit and you're saying that Milenko Trifunovic belonged to it. But he didn't. You are confusing the matter. That's one thing. And secondly, when you ask me if I know, then that's okay and then I'll answer, but you're putting things to me. You are saying "you know that" instead of saying "do you know that." That's the difference. At least this is how things are interpreted to me here. This is the interpretation that I'm receiving. I don't know whether this is your words or not. You can ask me whatever and what I know I will answer. I will never lie, but do not put words into my mouth. Do not tell me that I know things that I don't know. I don't have a single reason not to answer either you or anybody in the courtroom and tell you the truth. Whatever I know, I will tell you. However, if you're putting it to me that I know things that I don't know, please don't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'm asking my question also to give you the opportunity to explain whether you know or you don't know, et cetera --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, the following day, and we're talking about 14th at this point, you drove together with Momcilo Cvjetinovic and Milenko Canic to Pale and you drove from Bratunac, Konjevic Polje, and Pale. You passed by Kravica, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Of course we did. We had to pass through Kravica, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, did you notice anything in Kravica, or you passed by and you saw nothing?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know what I was supposed to notice in Kravica. Kravica was --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I'll tell you in a second what you're supposed --

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: -- destroyed on Christmas --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Let me tell you what I think you were supposed to see. Aleksandar Tesic is a Defence witness who testified in this case. Now, he was travelling along that road around noon on the 14th of July, and he testified in case that from the bus he was travelling, he saw a huge number of dead bodies lined up in front of the warehouse. In his testimony on 13 March at transcript page 35325, he said: "I figured there must have been at least between 200 and 300 bodies lying there piled about 1 metre and a half high." This is the first thing I'm asking you whether you noticed. Did you see a pile of bodies like Aleksandar Tesic?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see anything. I didn't see a pile of bodies. I didn't notice anything on the 14th on my way to Pale to visit President Radovan. I did not see anything, and that is the truth. As far as I'm concerned, this is correct. Perhaps he did see things I didn't. I don't know whether he was telling the truth or not. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Aleksandar Tesic also testified that the street in front of the Kravica warehouse was crammed with soldiers, making it difficult for the bus to move. So basically they were stuck in a sort of a traffic jam in front of the Kravica warehouse. And this is D03118 at paragraph 40. You didn't notice anything like this? You didn't notice a street crammed with soldiers when you passed by the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is no street. It's a road, a road between Bratunac, Konjevic Polje, on to Milici. There is no street. There was just the road. The only thing I noticed, if I recall correctly, was police or soldiers by the road. I didn't stop by. I didn't notice what Tesic said. It's his responsibility to say what he saw. I went by that road on the 14th, and I can tell you for a fact that there was no traffic jam there at the time I passed along that road. What Tesic saw and what stopped him, that was something he saw. If we had been there at the same time, I would tell him that there was no traffic jam of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, another witness for --

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: And let me just tell you --

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: You answered the question. If I may continue because we have very limited time. So another witness in this case, another Defence witness, Jovan Nikolic testified that the execution in front of the warehouse were still ongoing that day and that the bodies were moved and buried in Glogova, which you probably know is a little village on the same road that you were driving through. And this is D03126 at paragraphs 56 and 59. So we are talking about still the day you passed by, so the 14th of July, you passed by the Kravica warehouse. The day before one man from Skelani was killed and you were told that he was killed and something happened after. You were passing by. You didn't stop because you didn't think that there was any need for stopping and find out what happened to one of the men from your city, and in any event, you noted no crowd, no soldiers, no dead bodies, no killings, and no trucks. This is your testimony.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I observed soldiers. I observed people in police and military uniform by the road, but no lorries or anything like that. I passed through Kravica on the 14th. There was no traffic jam, and I did not notice anything else other than policemen and soldiers by the road, and that's exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, you also testified that obviously when you met with Karadzic, Deronjic, together with Canic and Cvjetinovic in Pale, you didn't discuss any of these issues. So while on the 11th for five or six Serbs killed, as you said in your interview, between the 9th and the 10th of July, you felt the need to drive all the way to Pale to discuss about these people killed, on the 14th there was no need to discuss any of these incidents, not a word.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I didn't go to Pale for the sake of five people who were killed and so I did have these discussions on -- for their sake, but I did not for the sake of those other unfortunates who were killed. No. I went to Pale because I was afraid that the front line would yield and that would result in the fall of Skelani, so don't make erroneous conclusions. Don't formulate things in an erroneous way. I didn't go to Pale for the sake of five people and then omitted to speak about 5.000 [as interpreted] people. That's not true. I went to Pale on the 11th because I was afraid that the line would yield and that Skelani would fall and that bad things would happen. So don't -- please don't put words into my mouth that I never uttered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, we were talking about your visit to Pale on the 14th of July, are we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the purpose of your visit has nothing to do with the front line of Skelani. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. That wasn't the reason why we went there on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Back to you, Mr. Costi.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted -- I was almost going to object to this question but if you see the question on lines 2, 3, and 4, Mr. Costi brought in the fact that the visit on the 11th had been for one purpose and was contrasting it for -- as to what might be discussed on the 14th, so I think that the witness's answer was responsive to that question, confusing as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yeah. That was -- that's what my understanding of the witness answer too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript, line 15. He didn't say "5.000," he said "thousands." "So I'm concerned for five people but not for thousands."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, can I have 65 ter 25103.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Mr. Katanic, this is -- the one you will see on the screen in a second is a picture that was taken in a demonstration or a rally organised by Momcilo Cvjetinovic in 1996 in Srebrenica in support of Ratko Mladic and Radovan Karadzic. Now, do you recognise yourself as the man standing behind the little kid with a cigarette in his mouth?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And do you recognise also Momcilo Cvjetinovic as the man on your left with a coloured shirt, black jacket, beard, smiling; correct?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course I recognise Momcilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And finally, the man squatting with the beard who makes the three finger signs is Milenko Canic; right?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: In the background over there you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: In the first row, squatting, with the white shirt and a long beard. Do you see Milenko Canic in the picture? Let me put it this way.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I guess it's him, but it's a bit ...

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I guess it's Milenko. His beard looks far darker and the man seems to be of heavier build than Milenko is really.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us what the sign board say?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: It says, "I'm a war criminal."

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Now, in his interview, Cvjetinovic explained that this Tribunal and the BiH corps are pretty much politicised and partial. If you want, I can read you the full passage, but this is literally one line of what he said. Do you agree with the statement?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, how should I know in what context Momcilo said that? If you take that sentence out of the whole context, you may in fact change the gist of what he wanted to say. So I can't comment on that one sentence unless I can see the entire conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Sure. I can give you the context. This is what he said at page 7 of his witness statement, which I don't think we don't need to brought up. I can simply read it to the transcript if Your Honour agree. At line 24 and 29 he said: "I personally do not deem him," Karadzic, "responsible for whatever, for all those things that he's been charged. To see at least I believe that he's as much guilty as the representatives of the other two nations in BiH which, as we can see, have managed that without being subject to any procedure, which, when I take a look at the result of the BiH court, brought me to the conclusion that both courts are pretty much politicised and partial." This is the full context. Would you agree with his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President, irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I will say, Your Honour, that it's relevant to the credibility of this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And -- and witness is only now getting translation. And witness is only now getting translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, obviously what I probably forgot to say, Mr. Cvjetinovic said this in context of later in the statement, then explaining the picture and the demonstration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Robinson's observation. We do not find it relevant. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Do you remember participating to the demonstration, though?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I have no idea where this is. I'm trying to recall where this is, and believe me, I don't know. I didn't take part in demonstrations frequently, but there you go. Here I am in the picture. What can I tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I think I'm up with my time and I don't have any other question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You're not tendering this photo?

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Yes. I will have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In your question you didn't hear -- you said demonstration, rally, organised by Momcilo Cvjetinovic in 1996 in Srebrenica in support of Mladic and Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And you didn't ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: Well, I asked the witness whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And your question is just whether he recognised himself and that's what we heard, "Yes, that's me." Since you're not giving evidence, I expected you put that to the witness. So, Mr. Katanic, I'm asking you whether you agree with Mr. Costi's statement that it was taken at a rally or demonstration in support of Mladic and Mr. Karadzic in 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I don't know where it was taken or when. I really don't know. If I did, there would be no reason for me not to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Although you don't know where it was taken and when it was taken, do you agree that it is part of demonstration in support of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the board -- reading the sign, well, it couldn't be anything else but a sign of support to Mr. Mladic and President Karadzic. I think that, though I don't know where and when or where this was, the gist of it was that it was a sign of support to President Karadzic and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive this. Shall we give the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6332.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Costi. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Several questions only.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Katanic, on page 60 you answered that in mid-April you went to work in Skelani. Can you tell us where it was from that you went to Skelani and from which work post?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I used to work in Srebrenica is as a director of the revenue administration of the municipality of Srebrenica, and I think it was sometime around the 14th, I think it was a Friday, that I went to Skelani to work as the chairman of the Executive Committee. So I was the director of the tax and revenue administration in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you familiar with the negotiations intended to create one or two municipalities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: This issue didn't arise in the cross-examination, whether there was a negotiation and the process through which the municipality was [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Whether it was not related to the issue, which municipality should be in charge of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. COSTI
utterances.text: I think there are two separate issue. Here we are talking about the establishment of the Skelani --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Just a second. I'll hear from the Defence. Mr. Karadzic, how did it arise from the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, the witness was told that he was banned from office. Second, he said that he went to the newly established municipality from -- and what he left was a job that he had been doing. He had not been laid off. And this was within the scope of Prosecutor's questions about his career. And we have a document about his appointment to the commission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll allow the question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was working in Srebrenica in the post of the director of the revenue administration in 1991 and 1992, the Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica was in the process of dividing the municipality into Skelani and Srebrenica. The Municipal Assembly set up a commission charged with the division of the municipalities, and I was a member -- one of the members of that commission charged with working out the division of the municipality of Srebrenica into the municipalities of Skelani and Srebrenica. Unfortunately, this never materialised because war hostilities broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that sanctions were imposed in 1998. What did you do from 1995 to 1998?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the Executive Board of the municipality of Srebrenica. When the authorities were set up in Srebrenica, I continued in the same post that I had in Skelani, and that was the president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you tell the Chamber what became of the municipality of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: The municipality of Skelani continued functioning post-1995. The same structures and duties that a municipality normally discharges existed in Skelani as well. I think it was in 2000 that the international community abolished the municipality of Skelani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the territory, under whose jurisdiction did it end up?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Under that of the municipality of Srebrenica. So again, Skelani and Srebrenica became a single territory in terms of it being a municipality with the seat in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And currently where are you working? You're occupying which post and in which municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I began working again in the municipality of Srebrenica as head of the department for the economy. Together with all the people living in Srebrenica, we are trying to contribute to some sort of prosperity for the Muslims and Serbs and everyone living in Srebrenica, to be able to earn a decent living, and that's the least that the people living there deserve, to have a better life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When sanctions were imposed on you, were you suspected of anything that was done during the war or post-Dayton? Why these sanctions?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I was not suspected of anything. I was sanctioned because, to tell you the truth, some sort of sub-appellate commission was there. It had to do with elections. There was only one piece of paper which said that I did things that were unheard of, but if you ask the people who were responsible for imposing this sanction on me why they did so, I don't think they would be able to tell you. I think that it had to do with the elections in 1997 in Srebrenica. Unfortunately, the Muslim Bosniak population was not present there. Some bags were brought over, and we were asked to accept the implementation of elections which were not in effect organised. As some sort of local official, I asked from the government, which was at the time was in Banja Luka, I asked the government or the Assembly to provide me with some sort of document. I even told categorically to a representative of the international community, Bring me a piece of paper from a cigarette box, anything, just give me something that would confirm my position as a local official that would entitle me, but I cannot confirm the legitimacy of the elections. This can only be been the government and parliamentary bodies. I tried to adhere to some sort of rules that were in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Aside from this political sanction, were you the subject of any criminal proceedings or conviction?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Well, under the pressure of the international community, I was accused of abuse of office, and some several years later, I don't know how many years later, five years, the charges were dismissed as unfounded and that's where it all ended. In other words, I was never convicted for anything and was never handed down with any sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you help us clarify the 13th now. On the 13th, in the morning, you were in Bratunac, at least that's what you told us. When did you leave Bratunac and go to Skelani?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Believe me, I don't know exactly. I know that it was in the afternoon that we returned to Skelani, but I can't tell you exactly when. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you observe in what direction the buses were headed? Were they arriving in Bratunac or were they passing through Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, a moment ago I said that I didn't observe them. I knew that people were charged with transporting the civilian population from Srebrenica and Bratunac to the territory of the federation. I knew that people were charged with that. But I didn't observe that. When I was heading toward the centre of town perhaps there were buses in the centre as the Prosecutor was saying, but I didn't observe it and I did not pay attention to it. The fact is that people were there so there must have been buses there. If people were being transported in the course of those days, then there must have been buses there, but to -- to tell you that I did observe them, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question. You were asked if you had heard of the executions at Kravica, at the Kravica warehouse. Did you hear that people were shot by firing squad there and executed or what exactly?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat what I heard, Mr. President. I heard that Krsto got killed and as a result there were problems, shooting, killings. I don't know to this very day how many were killed, whether there were executions or perhaps not. I really don't know. I never inquired. I only heard in the media. I read all sorts of things, but I officially never inquired. I never even asked Milenko Trifunovic or anybody else about that. I didn't ask him to tell me what happened, where, how, why. To this very day, if you have lie detectors, you can check if I'm telling the truth when I tell you that to this very day I don't know what happened and how. That's as far as I'm concerned. I'm not saying that things did not happen, that those things didn't happen, but I don't know. I can't say there were executions of which I knew because I didn't know. I don't know to this very day. Of course people were killed because they gone missing, but I don't know that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, can you tell us how did you understand this? Were you alarmed on the 13th when you heard about that event?

utterances.speaker: DANE KATANIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it was wartime. People get killed in war. Unfortunately, there was not just one Kravica. There were a lot of killings in 1992. We got hardened. How was I supposed to understand things? If you were a normal person, how could -- how could you react when you heard that people were getting killed? A person got killed. There was a situation, and a similar thing could happen the following day or if not worse. Things that were even worse happened before that. I'm not talking in percentages, but bad things happened from 1992 onwards. There was always something bad going on. It is not like we were living peacefully and then Kravica happened, which shocked us. Things were happening in continuity from 1992 onwards, and then finally when Croatia attacked us, all the people were taken away and they kept on killing. We just heard news about people who got killed, but war went on. People got killed, and you took it all in your stride. That's how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Katanic, for your testimony. Thank you for having come here. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That concludes your testimony, Mr. Katanic. On behalf of the Chamber, I thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You're now free to go. Given the time, we'll adjourn for today and continue tomorrow. The next witness is Mr. Kosoric, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
